extracted.intended_audience: novelists, literary critics, and educated readers interested in principles of fiction and humour
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts evaluative principles Chesterton uses to judge modern novelists and comic writing — what makes a novel true, comic, or morally and artistically sound. Useful for assessing or writing fiction, dialogue, and characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good novel vs bad novel
rubrics_metrics.description: A good novel tells us the truth about its hero; but a bad novel tells us the truth about its author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton contrasts sincerity in fiction (which reveals a coherent, truthful character-centred vision) with insincere books that reflect their maker more than their subject. Use this as a criterion: does the novel reveal the inner truth of its characters, or merely broadcast the author's temperament or affectations?

rubrics_metrics.name: Sociological value of bad literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Bad literature may tell us the mind of many men; a dishonest book is often honest as a public document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even poor or formulaic works (penny dreadfuls, halfpenny novelettes) have diagnostic value: they expose widespread assumptions and energies among readers and society. When evaluating literary works, consider whether their 'badness' nevertheless yields insight into popular beliefs or social spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid intellectual snobbishness/flattery of aristocracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The modern 'smart' aristocratic fiction flatters the gentry by ascribing exceptional wit and conversational power to them — a servile and false portrayal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chesterton criticizes novels that perform the 'essential function of flattery' by giving upper classes qualities (especially epigrammatic wit) they do not possess. As a standard: beware portraying social classes through flattering myths; prefer accuracy over flattering invention. Examples cited: Mrs. Craigie, 'Dodo', writers of the 'Smart Set'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic portrayal of social talk and wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit and epigrams are not the exclusive preserve of the aristocracy; the truly witty or talkative exchanges are often found among common people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dialogue and characterization should reflect realistic distributions of wit and speech. Do not attribute effortless repartee to nobles merely because they are nobles; assess whether conversational ability is plausible for a character's background. Chesterton notes that omnibus conductors may show more verbal felicity than peers in fashionable novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour must arise from unuttered joy, not empty frivolity
rubrics_metrics.description: The new frivolity is inadequate because there is in it no strong sense of an unuttered joy; characters joke not because merry but because not merry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate comic writing by whether its lightness springs from inner joy or merely masks emptiness. Repartee that comes from melancholy or affectation is inferior to repartee rooted in genuine mirth. Check for emotional source of humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courage to be sentimental (sentimentality as source of robust humour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Robust and uproarious humour has come from men capable of sentimentalism; the greatest comedians (Steele, Sterne, Dickens) combined violent innocence with comic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss sentimentality as automatically bad for comic effect. Chesterton argues that the capacity to be 'silly' or sentimental enables greater comic range and authenticity. When judging humour, consider whether an author has the courage to write sentimental or excessive moments that enable genuine laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelistic truth: narrative will and unpredictability
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel is truer than books of science or metaphysics because a story contains will and the necessity of events being settled for us without our permission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a creative principle, preserve elements of contingency and externally imposed limitation in plots and lives of characters. A novel gains romance and truth when not everything is under the protagonist's control; unexpected, uncontrollable circumstances keep life 'a story'. Evaluate whether a work allows fate/accident/limitation to shape drama rather than making the hero omnipotent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family as fertile source of drama and romance
rubrics_metrics.description: The family is wholesome because it contains divergencies and varieties; its uncongeniality supplies the bracing qualities of humanity and romance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In depicting domestic life, foreground the conflict, variety, and irrationality of relations rather than treating family as a cosy, homogeneous unit. The family should produce incidental, accidental, and dramatic forces that drive narrative and character growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fastidiousness and pretension of superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Fastidiousness (the pretence of being above common humanity) is a weakness; Nietzschean aristocracy of disdain is an 'aristocracy of weak nerves'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary tone or moral posture that prides itself on disdain for common people should be critiqued as a fault. Value humility, humour, and sympathy in authorship; treat scornful superiority as an anti-pattern in both character and narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic authenticity requires moral depth and humanity
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'good talk' (comic, humane conversation) requires friendship, honour, and abysmal tenderness; Johnsonian good talk comes from being a good man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging dialogue and comic scenes, check whether they rest on genuine moral warmth and humane feeling. Superficial cleverness without moral substance produces hollow comedy. Authors should cultivate personal decency and compassion to produce authentic comic dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject sterile rationalism and sad unreason
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern rationalism often yields a sad unreason; even their unreason is sad — an emptiness beneath their jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether an author's use of reason, irony, or scepticism leads to vitality or to a cold, lifeless tone. Prefer works where imagination, innocence, and 'gigantic' feeling balance intellect; avoid works where irony is merely defensive or disabling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exaggeration in popular romance can be honest admiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular halfpenny romances exaggerate beauty and courage (marquises seven feet high) but are not servile; their exaggeration is often an exuberant and honest admiration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that some forms of exaggeration or idealization in genre fiction are legitimate aesthetic choices expressing genuine admiration. When evaluating sensational or popular literature, differentiate between flattery-driven servility and imaginative exaggeration grounded in honest admiration.
